title: Chitrakoot
hook: Rama walks Sita around the mountain and tells her he doesn't miss the kingdom at all
tomorrow: Dasharatha's death and the curse that caused it (Shravana Kumara)

segments.voice: Yesterday: Chitrakoot today, a pilgrim town, and your line, reading the story with your feet. People still walk barefoot around Kamadgiri.

Every hard story has a pause, a stretch where the characters simply get to live. On Chitrakuta, the exiles get theirs. The hut is built. The days fall into a rhythm: bathing in the river, gathering fruit, sitting by the fire at night. And one day Rama takes Sita by the hand and walks her around the mountain, pointing things out, the way you'd show someone a neighborhood you've just moved into and already love.
screen: `EVERY HARD STORY HAS A PAUSE.` → `A RHYTHM TO THE DAYS.` → `SHOWING HER THE NEIGHBORHOOD.`

segments.voice: Look at the peaks, Rama tells Sita: some silver, some red, some gold, some the color of crystal. Look at the waterfalls, the flowering trees, the birds. Then he says something tender. Seeing this mountain with you, I don't grieve for the kingdom, and I don't miss my friends. Living here brings him two good things: he keeps his father's word, and he gives his brother Bharata joy. He takes her down to the Mandakini. The water is clear. Sages bathe in it, raising their arms to the sun, and deer come down to drink. Bathe here with me, he says. Think of this mountain as Ayodhya, the deer as its people, and the Mandakini as our own river Sarayu. You might hear an echo. Sumitra told Lakshmana: think of the forest as Ayodhya. Now Rama says it to Sita, and on the mountain, it's true. One honest note. Valmiki actually tells this scene a little later, while trouble is already on its way, and the contrast is part of his art. We've placed it here because it's the clearest picture of those first days. Now back to where Valmiki's story runs next. Far away, the charioteer Sumantra is driving into Ayodhya, alone, with an empty chariot. And an old king is waiting.
screen: `SILVER, RED AND GOLDEN PEAKS.` · `I DON'T GRIEVE FOR THE KINGDOM.` · `THE MANDAKINI IS OUR SARAYU.` · `THE CAMERA TURNS TO AYODHYA.` · then, large: `AN EMPTY CHARIOT GOES HOME.`

segments.voice: Pick one small place in your life where things are good right now: a corner, a routine, a person. On each breath in, notice one good detail about it; on each breath out, let it be enough, just as it is, for now.
Chitrakoot, the happy pause. Rama shows Sita the mountain and the Mandakini and tells her he doesn't miss the kingdom: this mountain is their Ayodhya now.
Your line: a hut on the hill. For a little while, the mountain is their Ayodhya. Day five hundred forty-one, done.

screen: `DAY 541 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: DASHARATHA'S DEATH AND THE CURSE.`

original.note: Sanskrit mandākinī: the river at Chitrakuta where Rama and Sita bathe; still the river of Chitrakoot town.

trapdoor: what you thought: the exile was misery from start to finish.
what it means: at Chitrakuta, Rama tells Sita he doesn't miss the kingdom at all.
what a scholar hears: Valmiki sets Rama's description of the mountain and the river just before Bharata's army arrives, so the happiest scene of the exile sits right beside the next shock.

chat.says: Was Rama miserable the whole time he was in exile?
options: Not on Chitrakuta: he told Sita he didn't miss the kingdom there with her.
Yes, he grieved for the kingdom every single day of the fourteen years.
He was only happy once Bharata came and offered him the throne back.
chat.meaning: On Chitrakuta Rama tells Sita he doesn't grieve for the kingdom: the mountain is their Ayodhya, the Mandakini their Sarayu.

Sarayu.meaning: the river of Ayodhya, Rama's home city

Sumitra.meaning: Lakshmana's mother, one of King Dasharatha's queens

Ayodhya.meaning: Rama's home city, capital of the kingdom
